newsitem.title: USA: GM parts workers strike; another walkout averted.
newsitem.headline: GM parts workers strike; another walkout averted.

text.p: Talks to end a new strike at General Motors Corp.'s Warren, Mich., transmission plant resumed Wednesday as union officials in Indiana rested after an early morning deal averted another parts plant walkout.
Some 2,800 hourly workers walked off the job at the Warren plant after a strike deadline expired at 11:59 p.m. EDT Tuesday.

The plant produces four-speed automatic transmissions for front-wheel-drive vehicles. The walkout -- the sixth against GM this year -- could force the automaker to idle several car and minivan assembly plants.
At risk are GM's new minivans and the Pontiac Grand Prix and Chevrolet Malibu sedans, new models that are critical to GM's drive to regain market share this year.

Bargainers for GM and United Auto Workers Local 909 resumed talks Wednesday morning in Warren. A GM spokeswoman declined to comment on the progress of the talks, which had snagged on the chronic issue of staffing levels and job security.

In Anderson, Ind., GM reached a tentative local labour agreement with UAW Local 663, preventing a strike at GM's Delphi Interior and Lighting Systems plant, which makes tail lamps and other lighting products for nearly every GM vehicle built in North America.
A strike at Anderson would quickly disrupt GM's production. A brief strike at the plant in 1994 forced GM to idle about 13 assembly plants within three days.
Local 663 officials said they expected the plant's 2,500 workers to vote on the contract deal next week.

"Did we get all we wanted? No, neither side got everything, but that's negotitations," said Local 663 President Ollie Dixon. "I do feel we achieved an agreement that the membership can live with. It addresssed the key issue of job security."

Last Friday, 5,850 workers from UAW Local 594 approved a settlement reached on July 16 with GM. The pact ended an 87-day strike at the Pontiac, Mich., full-size pickup truck plant. It was the longest walkout at GM in more than 25 years.
As part of the new accord, GM agreed to add 557 new production and skilled trades workers and pay a total of $9.5 million to settle grievances and cover missed holiday pay.

The Warren and Anderson strike deadlines were the most recent skirmishes between GM and the UAW. Union resistance to GM's efforts to cut its work force and send more work to outside contractors has led to a rancorous year of labour negotiations, including five strikes and numerous strike deadlines.

GM says it requires fewer workers to produce its newest generation of vehicles and needs to slash overall manufacturing costs to stay competitive. Union leaders insist that GM add more staffing to reduce overtime burdens and improve health and safety. The union also wants to bolster job security by forcing GM to limit how much work it sends to outside contractors.

A new national contract between GM and the UAW was signed last November. But the conflicts over staffing and outsourcing has led to slow bargaining progress. Of GM's 105 UAW locals, about 10 still do not have new contracts.
By contrast, the other members of Detroit's Big Three, Ford Motor Co. and Chrysler Corp., had their local contracts wrapped up months ago.
